title: Social Security Survivor Benefits: Who Qualifies and How Much
bigPicture: Social Security survivor benefits pay monthly money to eligible family members of someone who worked and paid Social Security taxes before they died.
whatYouNeedToKnow: You may qualify as a spouse, ex-spouse, child, or dependent parent of someone who worked and paid Social Security taxes before they died.

Spouses generally need to be age 60 or older (or 50 to 59 with a disability), to have been married at least 9 months, and not to have remarried before age 60 (age 50 with a disability). You might qualify at any age if you are caring for a child of the person who died.
Ex-spouses who were married at least 10 years may also qualify.
Children may qualify if they are unmarried and 17 or younger, or 18 to 19 and in school (K-12) full time, or any age if they developed a disability at age 21 or younger.
A dependent parent may qualify at age 62 or older if the child who died financially supported them.

Spouse payments start at 71.5% of the spouse's benefit and rise the longer you wait: over 75% at age 61, over 80% at 63, over 90% at 65, and up to 100% at Full Retirement Age for Survivor benefits (between 66 and 67).
Children generally get 75% of the parent's benefit, but a family maximum may lower everyone's payments.
If you qualify for Survivor benefits and another benefit, you choose the better one. They are not added together, and you can switch later.
Spouses or some minor children could also get a one-time $255 death payment.
commonMistakesToAvoid: Assuming survivor and retirement benefits add up. You choose one, not both.
Assuming you will get 100% right away. Payments start lower and rise with the age you start.
Assuming only older widows and widowers qualify. Children and some younger spouses can too.
Ignoring earnings limits. Your payment may be temporarily reduced if you earn above the limit.
actionSteps: Call Social Security at 1-800-772-1213 (TTY 1-800-325-0778), Monday through Friday, 8 a.m. to 7 p.m.
Have the Social Security number of the family member who died. If you do not have it, you will be asked for other details like their date of birth and parents' names.
A funeral home will usually report the death, so you may not need to.
Read the SSA pages listed below for the rules that fit your situation.
